title: Seeing the answer can make a study cue feel deceptively easy
body: In experiments reported in 2005, Asher Koriat and Robert Bjork found that people overestimated their future recall when judging a cue while the answer was visible. At test time, that extra information was gone.
takeaway: Estimate what you know from the prompt alone, in the same conditions you will face later.
source: Koriat and Bjork, Journal of Experimental Psychology (2005)
visual: a hand covering one half of an open page while reviewing

title: Four minutes of movement improved attention in one school study
body: A 2015 study tested short classroom activity breaks with children aged 9 to 11. On a measure of selective attention, pupils performed better after four minutes of interval activity than after a sedentary break.
takeaway: A break can occupy very little class time and still change how the next task begins.
source: Ma, Le Mare and Gurd, Applied Physiology, Nutrition, and Metabolism (2015)
visual: school pupils moving between desks during a short classroom break

title: Writing about exam worries helped in a 2011 study
body: Gerardo Ramirez and Sian Beilock asked students to write about worries just before taking a test. In their experiments, scores rose most clearly among students who usually felt anxious about exams.
takeaway: A short note can turn a diffuse worry into something you can name before returning to the task.
visual: a student writing privately at a desk before a test
